# Lab 5: Dimension reduction, clustering and annotation

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

## Notes

The estimated time for this lab is around 1h20.

:::

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}

## Aims

- Learn how to perform dimension reduction on scRNAseq data
- Understand the importance of feature selection
- Learn how to perform clustering on scRNAseq data
- Learn how to (automatically) annotate cells based on clustering results

:::

## Dimensional reduction for clustering

### Preparing dataset

We will prepare scRNAseq data from a PBMC run, provided by 10X and hosted by
`Bioconductor` as a package.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Which package from `Bioconductor` gives streamlined access to PBMC scRNAseq
dataset from 10X Genomics?

What does the object contain (type of data, number of cells, batches, organism,
...)? Can you get the same data from somewhere else?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
library(tidyverse)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
sce <- TENxPBMCData::TENxPBMCData('pbmc4k')
rownames(sce) <- scuttle::uniquifyFeatureNames(rowData(sce)$ENSEMBL_ID, rowData(sce)$Symbol_TENx)
sce
rowData(sce)
colData(sce)
table(sce$Library)
```

The counts are stored on disk, in a `HDF5` file (this is what the
`DelayedMatrix` class means): this is great to work with datasets which do not
fit in memory, but it is slower than working with an in-memory matrix. This
dataset is small enough to be loaded in memory, as a sparse matrix:

```{r filename = "R"}
counts(sce)
counts(sce) <- as(counts(sce), 'dgCMatrix')
counts(sce)[1:10, 1:10]
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Normalize counts using `scran`

Just like in bulk high-throughput sequencing experiments, scRNAseq counts have
to be normalized to the sequencing depth for each cell. We can define the
library size as the total sum of counts across all genes for each cell, the
expected value of which is assumed to scale with any cell-specific biases.
However, this relies on the assumption that within the entire dataset, most
genes are non-differentially expressed and expressed roughly within the same
range. Depending on the set up of the scRNAseq experiment, this can be entirely
false. To avoid relying on this hypothesis, we can (1) quickly pre-cluster cells,
then (2) normalize cells using their library size factor separately in each
cluster, then (3) rescaling size factors so that they are comparable across clusters.

All of this can be done very simply using the combo `quickCluster() + computeSumFactors()`
from the `scran` package, followed by `normalizeRnaCounts.se()` from the `scrapper` package.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

What is the purpose of the `quickCluster()` function? What does it return?

What is the purpose of the `computeSumFactors()` function? What does it return?

What is the purpose of the `normalizeRnaCounts.se()` function? What does it return?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
set.seed(1000)
clusters <- scran::quickCluster(sce)
table(clusters)
sce <- scran::computeSumFactors(sce, cluster = clusters)
colData(sce)
summary(sizeFactors(sce))
sce <- scrapper::normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce, size.factors = sizeFactors(sce))
assays(sce)
logcounts(sce)
```

`normalizeRnaCounts.se()` divides the counts of each cell by its size factor,
then log-transforms them (`log2(x + 1)`). Note that the `logcounts` assay is
not a regular matrix: it is a `LogNormalizedMatrix`, which only stores the
counts and the size factors, and computes the log-normalized values on the fly.
This saves a lot of memory for large datasets!

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Feature selection

We often use scRNAseq data in exploratory analyses to characterize heterogeneity
across cells. Procedures like clustering and dimensionality reduction compare
cells based on their gene expression profiles. The choice of genes to include in
this comparison may have a major impact on the performance of downstream methods.
Ideally, one wants to only select genes that contain useful information about
the biology of the system while removing genes that contain random noise.
This aims to preserve interesting biological structure without the variance
that obscures that structure.

The simplest approach to feature selection is to compute the variance of the
log-normalized expression values, to select the most variable genes.
Modelling of the mean-variance relationship can be achieved by the
`modelGeneVariances()` function from the `scrapper` package: it computes the
mean and the variance of the log-normalized expression of each gene, fits a
trend to the variance with respect to the mean (the *technical* variance), and
computes the residual from this trend for each gene (the *biological* variance).

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Apply the `modelGeneVariances()` function to the normalized counts. What does
the returned object contain?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
gene_variances <- scrapper::modelGeneVariances(logcounts(sce))
names(gene_variances)
gene_variances$statistics
```

:::
:::

Identify the top 10% most variable genes from this object.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
HVGs_idx <- scrapper::chooseHighlyVariableGenes(
    gene_variances$statistics$residuals,
    top = round(0.1 * nrow(sce))
)
HVGs <- rownames(sce)[HVGs_idx]
rowData(sce)$isHVG <- rownames(sce) %in% HVGs
head(rowData(sce))
table(rowData(sce)$isHVG)
```

`scrapper::chooseRnaHvgs.se()` performs both steps at once, and stores the
results in the `rowData()` of the `SingleCellExperiment` object.

:::
:::

Visualize the mean-variance fit of the data, coloring points by whether they are
in the top 10% most variable genes.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
df <- tibble(
    mean = gene_variances$statistics$means,
    var = gene_variances$statistics$variances,
    trend = gene_variances$statistics$fitted,
    HVG = rowData(sce)$isHVG
)
ggplot(df) +
    geom_point(aes(x = mean, y = var, col = HVG), alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_line(aes(x = mean, y = trend), col = 'darkred') +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(x = 'Gene mean exp. (norm.)', y = 'Gene exp. variance')
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### PCA on filtered dataset

We now have normalized counts filtered for the top 10% genes varying with the
greatest biological significance. Still, that represents a ~3,400 x nCells
(~4,300) dataset (each row being a feature). This is still too big to reliably
use in standard clustering approaches. We can further compress the dataset.
The most widely used approach is `PCA`: it computes a small number of
"components" (typically 5-50) optimally summarizing the variability of the
whole dataset, while retaining linearity of the underlying numerical data and
being computationallt quite efficient.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Use the `runPca.se()` function from the `scrapper` package to compute a `PCA`
embedding of the data, using the highly variable genes only.

How much of the variance is explained by each principal component? How many
components would you keep for downstream analyses?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
set.seed(1000)
sce <- scrapper::runPca.se(sce, features = rowData(sce)$isHVG, number = 50)
reducedDim(sce, 'PCA')[1:5, 1:5]
percent_var <- metadata(sce)$PCA$variance.explained / metadata(sce)$PCA$total.variance * 100
plot(percent_var, xlab = 'PC', ylab = 'Variance explained (%)', type = 'b')
```

The "elbow" of this curve suggests that the first ~15 PCs capture most of the
biological signal, and that the next ones mostly capture noise. We keep the
first 15 PCs for downstream analyses:

```{r filename = "R"}
reducedDim(sce, 'PCA') <- reducedDim(sce, 'PCA')[, 1:15]
p <- scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'PCA', colour_by = 'sizeFactor') + ggtitle('PCA')
p
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

## Clustering

Clustering is an unsupervised learning procedure that is used in scRNA-seq data
analysis to empirically define groups of cells with similar expression profiles.
Its primary purpose is to summarize the data in a digestible format for human
interpretation.

After annotation based on marker genes, the clusters can be treated as proxies for
more abstract biological concepts such as cell types or states. Clustering is thus a critical
step for extracting biological insights from scRNA-seq data.

### Clustering algorithms

Three main approaches can be used:

1. Hierarchical clustering
2. k-means clustering
3. Graph-based clustering

Today, we will focus on graph-based clustering, as it is becoming the standard
for scRNAseq: it is a flexible and scalable technique for clustering even the
largest scRNA-seq datasets. We first build a graph where each node is a cell
that is connected by edges to its nearest neighbors in the high-dimensional space.
Edges are weighted based on the similarity between the cells involved, with
higher weight given to cells that are more closely related.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Compute a graph-based clustering of the PBMC dataset.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
set.seed(1000)
graph <- bluster::makeSNNGraph(reducedDim(sce, 'PCA'), k = 5)
graph
sce_clust <- igraph::cluster_louvain(graph)$membership
sce$clusters_graph <- factor(sce_clust)
table(sce$clusters_graph)
```

The same can be achieved in a single step with `scrapper::clusterGraph.se()`,
which builds the shared nearest-neighbor graph from the `PCA` embedding and
clusters it with the "multilevel" (a.k.a. Louvain) algorithm:

```{r filename = "R"}
sce <- scrapper::clusterGraph.se(sce, num.neighbors = 5, method = "multilevel")
table(sce$clusters)
table(sce$clusters_graph, sce$clusters)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

What are the main parameters to choose when building the graph? How do they
impact the clustering?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
set.seed(1000)
graph2 <- bluster::makeSNNGraph(reducedDim(sce, 'PCA'), k = 50)
sce_clust2 <- igraph::cluster_louvain(graph2)$membership
table(sce_clust, sce_clust2)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Dimensional reduction for clustering visualization

`PCA` is a powerful linear approach to compress large datasets into smaller
dimensional spaces. However, it struggles at emphasizing the existence of
clusters in complex datasets, when visualized in 2D.

`scater` (and `scrapper`, with `runTsne.se()` and `runUmap.se()`) provides
a handy way to perform more complex data embeddings:

- tSNE
- UMAP
- Diffusion Map
- Multi-Dimensional Scaling (MDS)
- Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Explore the different dimensional reduction algorithms, trying different
hyperparameters combinations.

When you run these commands, pay attention to how long each command takes to
run! While this run, check the `Help` page for each function (e.g. `?runTSNE`)

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
set.seed(1000)
reducedDims(sce)
sce <- scater::runTSNE(sce, dimred = 'PCA')
sce <- scater::runUMAP(sce, dimred = 'PCA')
reducedDims(sce)
reducedDim(sce, 'UMAP')[1:10, ]
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Use the `scater::plotReducedDim()` function to plot cells in each embedding. Comment.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R", fig.width = 12, fig.height = 4}
library(patchwork)
p <- scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'PCA', colour_by = 'clusters_graph') + ggtitle('PCA') +
    scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'TSNE', colour_by = 'clusters_graph') + ggtitle('tSNE') +
    scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'UMAP', colour_by = 'clusters_graph') + ggtitle('UMAP')
p
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### [BONUS] For the pros of clustering... Compare different clustering approaches

Leveraging the `bluster` package, different clustering approaches can be
performed using a uniformed syntax, to compare their output.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Using `clusterSweep()`, compare the effect of different `k` neighbor values when
performing graph-based clustering.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R", fig.width = 10, fig.height = 12}
set.seed(1000)
clusters <- bluster::clusterSweep(
    reducedDim(sce, 'PCA'),
    BLUSPARAM = bluster::SNNGraphParam(),
    k = c(5L, 15L, 25L, 50L),
    cluster.fun = c("louvain")
)
colnames(clusters$clusters)
head(clusters$clusters)
clusters$parameters
library(ggraph)
p <- cowplot::plot_grid(
    clustree::clustree(
        as.data.frame(clusters$clusters) |> setNames(paste0('k', c(5, 15, 25, 50))),
        prefix = 'k',
        edge_arrow = FALSE
    ),
    cowplot::plot_grid(
        scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'TSNE', colour_by = I(clusters$clusters[, 'k.5_cluster.fun.louvain'])) + ggtitle('k = 5'),
        scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'TSNE', colour_by = I(clusters$clusters[, 'k.15_cluster.fun.louvain'])) + ggtitle('k = 15'),
        scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'TSNE', colour_by = I(clusters$clusters[, 'k.25_cluster.fun.louvain'])) + ggtitle('k = 25'),
        scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'TSNE', colour_by = I(clusters$clusters[, 'k.50_cluster.fun.louvain'])) + ggtitle('k = 50')
    ),
    nrow = 2,
    rel_heights = c(0.3, 0.7)
)
p
table(clusters$clusters[, 'k.5_cluster.fun.louvain'])
```

:::
:::

## Cell annotation

### Find marker genes

To interpret clustering results, one needs to identify the genes that drive
separation between clusters. These marker genes allow to assign biological
meaning to each cluster based on their functional annotation. In the most
obvious case, the marker genes for each cluster are *a priori* associated with
particular cell types, allowing us to treat the clustering as a *proxy* for cell
type identity.

A general strategy is to compare each cluster to each of the other clusters,
gene by gene, and then to combine the results of all these pairwise
comparisons into a single ranking of marker genes for each cluster.

Rather than p-values (which are not really meaningful here: the clusters were
defined from the very same data!), `scrapper::scoreMarkers.se()` computes
several *effect sizes* for each pairwise comparison:

- `cohens.d`: the difference in mean log-expression, divided by the standard deviation;
- `auc`: the probability that a random cell from the cluster has a higher expression than a random cell from the other cluster;
- `delta.mean`: the difference in mean log-expression (i.e. a log-fold change);
- `delta.detected`: the difference in the proportion of cells in which the gene is detected.

For each gene and each cluster, these effect sizes are then summarized across
all the pairwise comparisons (`min`, `mean`, `median`, `max`, `min.rank`).

```{r filename = "R"}
markers <- scrapper::scoreMarkers.se(sce, groups = sce$clusters_graph)
names(markers)
markers[[1]]
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Find the top markers of each cluster, ranking genes by their mean AUC across
all pairwise comparisons. Check `?scrapper::scoreMarkers.se` and
`?scrapper::previewMarkers` to find the right options to use.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
scrapper::previewMarkers(markers[[1]], order.by = 'auc.mean')
top_markers <- lapply(markers, function(df) {
    df <- df[order(df$auc.mean, decreasing = TRUE), ]
    rownames(df)[1:5]
})
top_markers
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Plot the expression of the first marker of the second cluster in tSNE.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
p <- scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'TSNE', colour_by = top_markers[[2]][[1]])
p
```

:::
:::

:::

### Automated cell annotation

Many cell type reference databases are available over the Internet.
Today, we will use a reference constructed from `Blueprint` and `ENCODE` data
(`Martens and Stunnenberg 2013`; `The ENCODE Project Consortium 2012`).
This reference is available from the `celldex` package as a
`SummarizedExperiment` containing log-normalized gene expression for manually
annotated samples.

```{r filename = "R"}
celldex::surveyReferences()
ref <- celldex::fetchReference("blueprint_encode", "2024-02-26")
ref
prediction_types <- SingleR::SingleR(
    test = sce,
    ref = ref,
    labels = ref$label.main
)
sce$annotation <- prediction_types$labels
table(sce$annotation)
table(sce$annotation, sce$clusters_graph)
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Using `scater` and `SingleR` utilities, visually compare the annotation scores
for cells in each cluster.

Did the automated annotation work robuslty? How does it compare to our
clustering? Is automated annotation as sensitive as graph-based clustering?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
p <- SingleR::plotScoreHeatmap(prediction_types)
p
p <- scater::plotReducedDim(sce, 'TSNE', colour_by = 'annotation') + ggtitle('Automated annotation')
p
p <- pheatmap::pheatmap(
    log2(table(Annotation = sce$annotation, Cluster = sce$clusters_graph)+10),
    color = colorRampPalette(c("white", "darkred"))(101)
)
```

:::
:::
